chunks: Where are my brethren who took the path and trod in rightness?
Where is ‘Ammār? And where is Ibn at-Tayyihān? And where is Dhu’sh-Shahādatayn?
And where are others like them from among their comrades who had pledged themselves to death and whose (severed) heads were taken to the wicked enemy.

key_terms.ابْنُ التَّيِّهَانِ: Ibn at-Tayyihān, a companion known for his piety.
key_terms.ذُو الشَّهَادَتَيْنِ: Dhu al-Shahadatayn (Possessor of the Two Testimonies), a title for ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir.
key_terms.عَمَّارٌ: ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir, a prominent companion known for his steadfastness.

ai.seo_question: Who are the specific companions mentioned in this reflection from Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this poignant passage from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (or the speaker) laments the absence of his steadfast companions—specifically ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir, Ibn al-Tayyāhān, and Dhu al-Shahadatayn—who exemplified the Shia ideal of *shahāda* (martyrdom) through their unwavering commitment to truth. This rhetorical questioning serves not only as a historical reflection on the early Islamic community but also as a theological anchor for the concept of *al-Mahdi*, linking the legacy of the faithful to the eventual emergence of the Awaited Imam. The mention of their heads being sent to the enemies underscores the physical cost of their fidelity, reinforcing the Shia narrative of sacrifice as a path to divine proximity.
